issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette: Arjun was twenty-three when the studio fire swallowed the south wall of his first firm’s workspace. He had been layout-ready, waiting for the senior art director to review his proofs. When the electrical panel sparked, the air turned thick with acrid, scorched insulation. Sirens wailed within minutes, and uniformed officers filled the doorway, shouting orders that overlapped into a single, unintelligible roar. In the chaos, the art director someone Arjun had trusted to guide him slipped out a side exit, leaving Arjun to navigate the smoke and the arriving responders alone. The firefighters contained the blaze, but the silence that followed felt heavier than the noise. Arjun walked home with soot on his cuffs and a hollow certainty that he had somehow failed to protect the work, the space, or himself. For weeks after, the studio’s ventilation carried faint traces of burnt plastic that made Arjun’s breath catch. He held his breath when a colleague microwaved fish or when the building’s old furnace kicked on. The first time a neighborhood patrol car rolled past his apartment, he found himself pressed against the glass, tracking every movement. Uniforms on the street, on a television, anywhere he looked his eyes followed them automatically. He began rehearsing what he would say to clients before he even opened his laptop. He would stand in his kitchen, practicing the cadence of a project pitch until his throat ached, certain that one misstep would unravel everything. When the event surfaced in his mind, a wave of guilt would rise before he could name it. He knew the sequence of events clearly enough to trace the timeline, but the moment he tried to put it into words, the sentences fractured. He would stop mid-explanation during dinner with his wife, Elena, his voice catching as he lost the thread. He knew what happened, yet the words simply would not form. The betrayal lingered alongside the guilt the director’s quiet exit, the way the responding officers had initially read his soot-stained clothes as reckless behavior. People, he had come to believe, could not be trusted to see him clearly. The world felt inherently precarious, a place where authority figures could shift from protectors to threats in a single breath. His work as a graphic designer became a series of managed encounters. Clients who wore structured blazers or official-looking lanyards made his pulse jump. He avoided scheduling work beyond two weeks, telling himself it was efficient, though the truth was that drafting anything further ahead required imagining a tomorrow where the ground did not suddenly give way. When his building management sent out an email about a routine safety inspection, Arjun spent the weekend drafting and deleting three separate replies, each time stepping away from his monitor before hitting send. He stopped booking weekend trips, canceling reservations the moment he realized he was picturing unfamiliar faces in uniform. His design pipeline thinned. Meetings were shortened. He learned to sit with his back to the door, scanning the entryway every time the elevator dinged. At forty-one, Arjun sits in a quiet therapy office, his hands resting flat on his knees. It was the anniversary of the fire, combined with a stalled project due to his inability to commit to a launch timeline, that finally brought him through the door. He is afraid that if he lets someone in, he will lose his composure again, that the words will fail him mid-sentence. What he hopes for is quieter than he dares to say: a way to look at a burnt coffee filter or a police cruiser without his chest tightening, and to trust that he can navigate the next client meeting without losing himself in the rehearsal. He wants to stop bracing for a betrayal that no longer exists, even though the memory of it still sits heavy in his chest.
